Set
$$
\mathbb F_2:=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z=\{[0]_2,[1]_2\},
$$
with addition and multiplication induced by the quotient operations
$$
[r]_2+[s]_2=[r+s]_2,\qquad [r]_2[s]_2=[rs]_2
$$
from [[def-addition-and-multiplication-modulo-n]]. This item fixes the two residue classes and their operations. It does not assert the field axioms; those must be established separately before an argument uses field properties.

Let $p \in \mathbb{Z}$ ([[def-integers]]), ordered as in [[def-int-order]], with
divisibility as in [[def-divides-in-z]]. Then $p$ is **prime** when

$$p > 1 \qquad \text{and} \qquad d \mid p \ \text{ with } \ d > 0 \ \text{ force } \ d = 1 \ \text{ or } \ d = p .$$

In words: $p$ exceeds $1$, and its only positive divisors are $1$ and $p$. An
integer $n$ with $n > 1$ that is not prime is **composite**; unfolding the
definition, $n$ is composite exactly when $n > 1$ and $n$ has a positive divisor
$d$ with $d \ne 1$ and $d \ne n$.

**Numerals.** For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ the symbol $k$ inside $\mathbb{Z}$ means
$\iota(k)$, the embedding of [[lem-nat-embeds-int]]; in particular $0$ and $1$
are the ring constants of [[def-int-operations]].

**Boundary values, stated rather than assumed.** $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]) and $\mathbb{Z}$ contains $0$, $1$ and the negatives,
so the small cases are recorded explicitly. The clause $p > 1$ decides all of
them at once:

- $1$ is **not** prime, since $1 > 1$ is false, and not composite either, since
  composite also requires $n > 1$.
- $0$ is **not** prime, since $0 > 1$ is false. This is decided by the size
  clause alone and not by counting divisors: every integer divides $0$
  ([[def-divides-in-z]]), so the divisor condition is not what rules $0$ out.
- Every negative integer is neither prime nor composite, again because $p > 1$
  fails. So a prime is in particular positive, and $-2$, $-3$, $-5$ are not
  primes in this library, though each is $-1$ times one.

Thus "prime" and "composite" between them classify exactly the integers greater
than $1$, and nothing else.

**The same condition read over all divisors.** For $p > 1$ the following are
equivalent:

1. the only positive divisors of $p$ are $1$ and $p$;
2. the only divisors of $p$ are $1$, $-1$, $p$ and $-p$.

That 2 implies 1 is immediate, since of those four only $1$ and $p$ are positive
($p > 1 > 0$, so $-1 < 0$ and $-p < 0$). For the converse let $d \mid p$. Since
$p > 1$ we have $p \ne 0$, so $d \ne 0$ by [[lem-divisor-bound]]; and
$|d| \mid p$, because $|d|$ is $d$ or $-d$ ([[def-int-abs]]) and those two divide
$p$ together ([[lem-divisibility-basic]]). Also $|d| \ge 0$ and $|d| \ne 0$
([[lem-int-abs-properties]]), so $|d| > 0$ and clause 1 gives $|d| = 1$ or
$|d| = p$. If $|d| = 1$ then $d = 1$ or $d = -1$, by the case split defining
$|d|$; and if $|d| = p = |p|$ then $d = up$ for a unit $u \in \{1,-1\}$
([[lem-associates-characterisation]], [[lem-units-of-z]]), that is $d = p$ or
$d = -p$. Both readings are used below without further comment.

**Why $1$ is excluded, and it is not a matter of taste.** The exclusion is
forced by the uniqueness half of [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-arithmetic]],
proved on this page: if $1$ counted as a prime, a factorisation could be padded
with any number of factors $1$, so lists of different lengths would represent
the same integer and no permutation could match them. Existence of a
factorisation would survive the change; it is uniqueness alone that fixes the
convention, and the explicit witness is recorded on the companion page.

For every prime $p$, the operations of addition and multiplication on
$\mathbb Z/p$ make it a field ([[def-field]]).

Set
$$
\mathbb F_2:=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z=\{[0]_2,[1]_2\},
$$
with addition and multiplication induced by the quotient operations
$$
[r]_2+[s]_2=[r+s]_2,\qquad [r]_2[s]_2=[rs]_2
$$
from [[def-addition-and-multiplication-modulo-n]]. This item fixes the two residue classes and their operations. It does not assert the field axioms; those must be established separately before an argument uses field properties.

The quotient operations on $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ make the carrier $\mathbb F_2$ of [[def-qa-binary-field-f2]] a field. This is only the modulus-$2$ specialization of the published prime-modulus theorem; it does not assert a classification of finite fields.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), with additive identity $0_F$, multiplicative
identity $1_F$, and the field axioms as stated there. A **vector space over $F$**,
also called an **$F$-vector space**, consists of

- a set $V$, whose elements are called **vectors**;
- a binary operation $+ : V \times V \to V$ on $V$ ([[def-binary-operation]]),
  the **vector addition**;
- an element $0_V \in V$, the **zero vector**;
- a map $\cdot \,:\, F \times V \to V$, the **scalar multiplication**, written
  $\lambda v := \cdot(\lambda, v)$;

subject to the following axioms, in which $u, v \in V$ and $\lambda, \mu \in F$
are arbitrary.

- **(V1)** $(V, +, 0_V)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]): $+$ is associative
  and commutative, $0_V$ is a two-sided identity for $+$
  ([[def-identity-element]]), and every $v \in V$ has an additive inverse
  ([[def-invertible-element]]).
- **(V2)** $\lambda(u + v) = \lambda u + \lambda v$.
- **(V3)** $(\lambda + \mu)v = \lambda v + \mu v$.
- **(V4)** $(\lambda\mu)v = \lambda(\mu v)$.
- **(V5)** $1_F v = v$.

The elements of $F$ are called **scalars**. When several vector spaces are in
play we write $0_V$ for the zero of $V$, and we write $-v$ for the additive
inverse of $v$ and $u - v := u + (-v)$.

**The notation $0_V$ and $-v$ is legitimate.** Axiom (V1) asserts only that some
two-sided identity and some additive inverses exist. That there is at most one
two-sided identity for $+$ is [[lem-identity-unique]], and that an invertible
element of a monoid has exactly one inverse is [[lem-inverse-unique]]; both are
proved before [[def-group]] and are inherited here with the group structure. So
$0_V$ and $-v$ denote well-defined elements, and nothing below re-derives them.

**What (V1) buys, and why it is not restated.** Associativity, commutativity, the
identity law $v + 0_V = v = 0_V + v$, the inverse law $v + (-v) = 0_V$,
cancellation ([[lem-group-cancellation]]) and the inverse identities
([[lem-group-inverse-laws]]) are facts about abelian groups. They are quoted from
the group page wherever they are used and are never proved again for vectors.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]). As in
[[def-linear-combination-and-span]], a **finite list** of vectors is a function
$v : n \to V$ on a von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), written
$v_i := v(i)$, and

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$$

is the finite sum of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] read additively in the abelian
group $(V,+,0_V)$, applied to the list $i \mapsto \lambda_i v_i$. No second notion
of finite sum is introduced here.

### Independence of a list

A finite list $v : n \to V$ is **linearly independent** when, for every list of
scalars $\lambda : n \to F$,

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i = 0_V \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \lambda_i = 0_F \text{ for every } i < n,$$

and **linearly dependent** otherwise, that is, when some $\lambda : n \to F$ has
$\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i = 0_V$ while $\lambda_j \ne 0_F$ for at least one
$j < n$. Such a $\lambda$ is called a **witness** to the dependence of $v$.

### Independence of a subset

A subset $S \subseteq V$ is **linearly independent** when **every injective**
finite list $v : n \to S$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]) is linearly
independent, and **linearly dependent** otherwise, that is, when some injective
finite list into $S$ is linearly dependent.

**The injectivity clause is not decoration.** A linear combination in
[[def-linear-combination-and-span]] is indexed by an arbitrary list $v : n \to S$,
which is **not** required to be injective. If the definition above quantified
over all such lists, then for any $w \in S$ the list $v : 2 \to S$ with
$v_0 = v_1 = w$ and the scalars $\lambda_0 = 1_F$, $\lambda_1 = -1_F$ would give

$$\sum_{i<2}\lambda_i v_i = (0_V + 1_F w) + (-1_F)w = w + (-w) = 0_V$$

with $\lambda_0 = 1_F \ne 0_F$ ([[def-field]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), so **every** nonempty subset of
$V$ would be dependent and the notion would be empty. Quantifying over injective
lists is what makes the subset notion the intended one. It costs nothing for
lists: [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]] shows that the vanishing condition
above already forces a list to be injective, so no injectivity hypothesis has to
be carried alongside independence of a list.

### The boundary cases are genuine cases

$\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so both of the following are
instances of the definitions and neither is a convention.

- **The empty list is independent.** For $n = 0$ the only list of scalars is the
  empty one, and the condition "$\lambda_i = 0_F$ for every $i < 0$" holds
  vacuously.
- **$\varnothing \subseteq V$ is independent.** The only function $v : n \to
  \varnothing$ is the empty one, with $n = 0$, and it is independent by the
  previous point.
- **$\{0_V\}$ is dependent.** The list $v : 1 \to \{0_V\}$ with $v_0 = 0_V$ is
  injective, and taking $\lambda_0 = 1_F$ gives
  $\sum_{i<1}\lambda_i v_i = 0_V + 1_F 0_V = 0_V$ by the recursion of
  [[def-monoid-finite-product]] and $\lambda 0_V = 0_V$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), while $1_F \ne 0_F$ in a field
  ([[def-field]]). So $\{0_V\}$, and hence every subset of $V$ containing $0_V$,
  is linearly dependent.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

### Finite sums of vectors

By axiom (V1) the triple $(V, +, 0_V)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]), hence
in particular a commutative monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]). So the finite
products of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] are available in it, and we write them
**additively**: for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a finite list $u : n \to V$, that is a
function on the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]),

$$\sum_{i<n} u_i \;:=\; \prod_{i<n} u_i \quad \text{computed in } (V,+,0_V),$$

so that $\sum_{i<0} u_i = 0_V$ and $\sum_{i<\sigma(n)} u_i = \bigl(\sum_{i<n} u_i\bigr) + u_n$,
and the value depends only on $u_0, \dots, u_{n-1}$.

### Linear combinations

A **linear combination in $V$** is a vector of the form

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$$

where $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ is a finite list of scalars and
$v : n \to V$ is a finite list of vectors; the sum is the finite sum just
described, of the list $i \mapsto \lambda_i v_i$. For $S \subseteq V$, a vector
$w \in V$ is a **linear combination of elements of $S$** when there are
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ and $v : n \to S$ with
$w = \sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$.

**The empty case is a real case.** $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]), and at $n = 0$ the sum is the empty sum, which is
$0_V$. So $0_V$ is a linear combination of elements of every subset of $V$,
including $S = \varnothing$. The lists are indexed from $0$, so a linear
combination of length $n$ is $\lambda_0 v_0 + \dots + \lambda_{n-1}v_{n-1}$; no
statement here is restricted to $n \ge 1$.

### The span

Let $S \subseteq V$. The set of linear subspaces of $V$ containing $S$ is
nonempty, since $V$ itself is one, so its intersection is a linear subspace of
$V$ by [[lem-intersection-of-linear-subspaces]]. That intersection is the **span
of $S$**,

$$\operatorname{span}(S) \;:=\; \bigcap \{\, W \;:\; W \text{ is a linear subspace of } V \text{ and } S \subseteq W \,\} .$$

It contains $S$, being an intersection of sets each of which contains $S$, and it
is contained in every linear subspace of $V$ that contains $S$. So it is the
**smallest** linear subspace of $V$ containing $S$, and those two properties
determine it uniquely: if $W$ and $W'$ both contain $S$ and are each contained in
every linear subspace containing $S$, then each is contained in the other. This
is what licenses the definite article.

A subset $S \subseteq V$ **spans** $V$, or is a **spanning set** of $V$, when
$\operatorname{span}(S) = V$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) and let
$S \subseteq V$. Write

$$L(S) \;:=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i \;:\; n \in \mathbb{N},\ \lambda : n \to F,\ v : n \to S \,\Bigr\}$$

for the set of linear combinations of elements of $S$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]). Then

$$\operatorname{span}(S) \;=\; L(S).$$

In particular $\operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$, and for every
$S \subseteq V$ the span of $S$ contains $0_V$ as the empty linear combination.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

A subset $B \subseteq V$ is a **basis of $V$** when

- **(B1)** $B$ is linearly independent ([[def-linear-independence]]), and
- **(B2)** $B$ spans $V$, that is $\operatorname{span}(B) = V$
  ([[def-linear-combination-and-span]], which is where the words *spans* and
  *spanning set* are fixed; they are not redefined here).

**The empty set is a basis of the zero space, and of nothing else.**
$\varnothing$ is linearly independent ([[def-linear-independence]]) and
$\operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]]), so $\varnothing$ is a basis of
$V$ exactly when $V = \{0_V\}$. This is the case $n = 0$ from which every
induction on this page starts, and it is a genuine case rather than a convention.

### Ordered bases

An **ordered basis of $V$** is a finite list $v : n \to V$, with $n \in
\mathbb{N}$ and $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ the von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), such that $v$ is
injective ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]) and its image $v[n]$ is a
basis of $V$.

By claim 6 of [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]], a list is linearly
independent exactly when it is injective with linearly independent image, so an
ordered basis is equally described as a **linearly independent list $v : n \to V$
with $\operatorname{span}(v[n]) = V$**: the injectivity does not have to be
imposed separately. The empty list is the ordered basis of the zero space.

An ordered basis is a list, so it carries an order; a basis is a set, so it does
not. Reordering an ordered basis gives a different ordered basis with the same
image, and the coordinates of
[[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] are attached to the
list, not to the set.

### Bases of a linear subspace

Let $U$ be a linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]), which is itself a
vector space over $F$, with the addition, the zero vector and the scalar
multiplication of $V$ restricted to $U$. For $A \subseteq U$ the two readings of
"$A$ is a basis" — computed inside $U$, or computed inside $V$ — agree, so the
phrase needs no disambiguation below.

- **Independence agrees.** The finite sums $\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i a_i$ of a list
  $a : n \to U$ are given by the same recursion in $U$ as in $V$
  ([[def-monoid-finite-product]]), the base value $0_V$ and the operation $+$
  being literally those of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). So a list into $U$ has
  the same sums whichever space it is read in, and the vanishing condition of
  [[def-linear-independence]] is the same condition in both.
- **The span agrees.** A subset of $U$ is a linear subspace of $U$ exactly when it
  is a linear subspace of $V$, conditions (W1), (W2), (W3) being the same
  conditions in either reading. Now $\operatorname{span}_V(A) \subseteq U$, since
  $U$ is a linear subspace of $V$ containing $A$ and the span is contained in
  every such subspace; so $\operatorname{span}_V(A)$ is a linear subspace of $U$
  containing $A$, whence $\operatorname{span}_U(A) \subseteq \operatorname{span}_V(A)$.
  Conversely $\operatorname{span}_U(A)$ is a linear subspace of $V$ containing
  $A$, whence $\operatorname{span}_V(A) \subseteq \operatorname{span}_U(A)$. The
  two are therefore equal, and we write $\operatorname{span}(A)$ for both.

Consequently $A \subseteq U$ is a basis of the vector space $U$ if and only if
$A$ is linearly independent as a subset of $V$ and $\operatorname{span}(A) = U$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

$V$ is **finite-dimensional over $F$** when it has a **finite** basis
([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-countable]]): some basis $B$ of $V$ satisfies
$B \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]).

For such a $V$, the **dimension of $V$ over $F$**, written $\dim_F V$, is that
$n$:

$$\dim_F V \;:=\; \text{the unique } n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } V \text{ has a basis } B \text{ with } B \approx n .$$

**This is well defined.** Existence of such an $n$ is the hypothesis, together
with the fact that a finite set is equinumerous with exactly one natural number
([[lem-pigeonhole]], claim 3). Uniqueness is
[[thm-any-two-finite-bases-have-the-same-size]]: two bases of $V$ with $n$ and
with $m$ elements force $n = m$. That theorem is therefore a **prerequisite** of
this definition, not a later justification of it, and it is listed in `deps`.

$V$ is **infinite-dimensional over $F$** when it is not finite-dimensional over
$F$, that is, when $V$ has **no** finite basis. No number is attached to such a
space here: the symbol $\dim_F V$ is defined only in the finite-dimensional case,
and the expression $\dim_F V = \infty$ is not used.

**The zero space.** $\varnothing$ is a basis of $\{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-basis]]) and $\varnothing \approx 0$, so $\{0_V\}$ is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F \{0_V\} = 0$. Conversely a space of dimension $0$
has a basis $B \approx 0$, that is $B = \varnothing$, and then
$V = \operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

derivations.claim: The coordinate operations are closed because each coordinate operation is an operation in $\mathbb F_2$ by [F1]. Each vector-space axiom in [F2] holds coordinate by coordinate by the corresponding field axiom in [F1]; coordinatewise equality then gives the vector identity. For $n=0$ there is only the empty tuple, and all coordinate identities hold vacuously.

For $i<n$, let $e_i$ have coordinate $1$ at $i$ and $0$ elsewhere. Every $x\in\mathbb F_2^n$ equals $\sum_{i<n}x_i e_i$ coordinatewise, so $B=\{e_i:i<n\}$ spans. The vectors $e_i$ are pairwise distinct because their $1$-coordinates differ. To verify that $B$ is independent in the subset sense of [F3], take any finite injective list $b:r\to B$ and coefficients $c_t\in\mathbb F_2$. If $r=0$, the independence implication is vacuous. Otherwise write $b_t=e_{i_t}$; injectivity and distinctness of the $e_i$ make the indices $i_t$ pairwise distinct. The coordinate $i_t$ of $\sum_{u<r}c_u b_u$ is then exactly $c_t$, so a zero sum forces every $c_t=0$. This also covers $n=0$, since then $B=\varnothing$ admits no nonempty list. Thus $B$ is independent, and it is a basis by [F4]–[F5]. Its $n$ distinct vectors give dimension $n$.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space with the root pairing linear in its first argument, and let $u\in H$ satisfy $\|u\|=1$. Define $P_u:=|u\rangle\langle u|$ by the root-linear-first Dirac convention. Then $P_u$ is self-adjoint and idempotent, has one-dimensional range, is non-negative, and has trace one. In particular, $P_u$ is a density operator.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Its **endomorphisms** are its complex-linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]); for an endomorphism $P$, $P^*$ denotes its adjoint, which exists uniquely in finite dimension ([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]], [[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]]). A **finite projective measurement** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $(P_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ of endomorphisms such that

$$P_a^*=P_a,\qquad P_a^2=P_a,\qquad P_aP_b=0\ (a\ne b),\qquad \sum_{a\in\Omega}P_a=I_H.$$

The products above are compositions, the sum is pointwise addition of endomorphisms, and $I_H$ is the identity map; these operations preserve linear maps ([[prop-linear-maps-form-a-vector-space]], [[lem-composition-and-identity-linear-maps]]). The projections $P_a=0$ are permitted. For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (nonnegative and trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), the associated outcome weights are $p_\rho(a)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_a)$; their nonnegativity and normalization are proved in [[thm-qc-projective-measurement-outcome-law]].

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space; the pairing is linear in its first argument ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for its complex-linear endomorphisms ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]) and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite POVM** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $E=(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ with each $E_a$ nonnegative and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}E_a=I_H$; after any enumeration of $\Omega$, these operators form the finite complete positive family of [[def-qc-finite-positive-effect-family]]. Reordering does not alter the finite sum. The complete-family lemma [[lem-qc-complete-effect-family-members-are-effects]] shows that every $E_a$ also has nonnegative complement $I_H-E_a$, so each is an effect.

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (a nonnegative operator of trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), its **POVM outcome weights** are

$$p_\rho(a):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a),\qquad a\in\Omega.$$

Here $\operatorname{tr}$ is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

The positivity and normalization of these weights are proved in [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]]. A POVM specifies this outcome law; it does not by itself prescribe a conditional output state.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

citations.quote:
Fix integers $n\ge1$ and $m\ge n-1$. A total function $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^m$ satisfies the **Simon hidden-XOR-period promise** if there is a unique nonzero string $s\in\{0,1\}^n$ such that for all $x,y\in\{0,1\}^n$,

$$f(x)=f(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (y=x\text{ or }y=x\oplus s).$$

For the query algorithms using this promise, the instance is $n,m$ together with black-box access to $f$: the solver receives no function table or other information depending on $f$. Each oracle call uses the standard bit-query interface [[def-qa-standard-bit-query]]. Its witness relation $R(f,s)$ holds exactly when $s$ is the nonzero mask in the displayed iff condition, so the required output is the unique hidden mask. The address operation $\oplus$ is the coordinatewise addition of [[def-qa-binary-field-f2]]. The output width condition lets the $2^{n-1}$ fibers receive distinct labels; it does not promise that the image uses every $m$-bit label. Each fiber is exactly $\{x,x\oplus s\}$.

For $n\ge0$, let $\mathbb F_2^n=\{0,1\}^n$. Give it coordinatewise addition $(x+y)_i=x_i+y_i$ and scalar multiplication $(c x)_i=cx_i$ using the operations of [[def-qa-binary-field-f2]]. Its zero vector is $0^n$. Then $\mathbb F_2^n$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F_2$, with standard basis $e_0,\ldots,e_{n-1}$ and dimension $n$. For $n=0$, the carrier consists of the empty tuple, and the basis is empty.

The quotient operations on $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ make the carrier $\mathbb F_2$ of [[def-qa-binary-field-f2]] a field. This is only the modulus-$2$ specialization of the published prime-modulus theorem; it does not assert a classification of finite fields.

For $n\ge0$ and $a,x\in\{0,1\}^{n}$, define the one-bit **binary dot product**
$$
a\cdot x:=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{n-1}(a_i\land x_i),
$$
where $\land$ is Boolean conjunction and $\bigoplus$ is the left-to-right fold of XOR, with empty fold $0$. It is the parity of the number of coordinates where both bits are $1$. Under the quotient operations of [[def-qa-binary-field-f2]], this bit represents the sum $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}[a_i]_2[x_i]_2$ in $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$; the equality uses only the operation definitions, not the field axioms.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), with additive identity $0_F$, multiplicative
identity $1_F$, and the field axioms as stated there. A **vector space over $F$**,
also called an **$F$-vector space**, consists of

- a set $V$, whose elements are called **vectors**;
- a binary operation $+ : V \times V \to V$ on $V$ ([[def-binary-operation]]),
  the **vector addition**;
- an element $0_V \in V$, the **zero vector**;
- a map $\cdot \,:\, F \times V \to V$, the **scalar multiplication**, written
  $\lambda v := \cdot(\lambda, v)$;

subject to the following axioms, in which $u, v \in V$ and $\lambda, \mu \in F$
are arbitrary.

- **(V1)** $(V, +, 0_V)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]): $+$ is associative
  and commutative, $0_V$ is a two-sided identity for $+$
  ([[def-identity-element]]), and every $v \in V$ has an additive inverse
  ([[def-invertible-element]]).
- **(V2)** $\lambda(u + v) = \lambda u + \lambda v$.
- **(V3)** $(\lambda + \mu)v = \lambda v + \mu v$.
- **(V4)** $(\lambda\mu)v = \lambda(\mu v)$.
- **(V5)** $1_F v = v$.

The elements of $F$ are called **scalars**. When several vector spaces are in
play we write $0_V$ for the zero of $V$, and we write $-v$ for the additive
inverse of $v$ and $u - v := u + (-v)$.

**The notation $0_V$ and $-v$ is legitimate.** Axiom (V1) asserts only that some
two-sided identity and some additive inverses exist. That there is at most one
two-sided identity for $+$ is [[lem-identity-unique]], and that an invertible
element of a monoid has exactly one inverse is [[lem-inverse-unique]]; both are
proved before [[def-group]] and are inherited here with the group structure. So
$0_V$ and $-v$ denote well-defined elements, and nothing below re-derives them.

**What (V1) buys, and why it is not restated.** Associativity, commutativity, the
identity law $v + 0_V = v = 0_V + v$, the inverse law $v + (-v) = 0_V$,
cancellation ([[lem-group-cancellation]]) and the inverse identities
([[lem-group-inverse-laws]]) are facts about abelian groups. They are quoted from
the group page wherever they are used and are never proved again for vectors.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]). A subset
$W \subseteq V$ is a **linear subspace** of $V$ when

- **(W1)** $0_V \in W$;
- **(W2)** $W$ is closed under the vector addition: $u, v \in W$ implies
  $u + v \in W$;
- **(W3)** $W$ is closed under scalar multiplication: $\lambda \in F$ and
  $v \in W$ imply $\lambda v \in W$.

Every vector space $V$ has the two **trivial linear subspaces** $\{0_V\}$ and $V$
itself; a linear subspace $W$ with $W \ne V$ is called **proper**.

**The restricted operations are the required data, and $W$ is a vector space.**
By (W2) the vector addition of $V$ restricts to a binary operation
$W \times W \to W$, and by (W3) the scalar multiplication restricts to a map
$F \times W \to W$. With these and the element $0_V$, the set $W$ is a vector
space over $F$:

- axioms (V2)–(V5) are equations required of elements of $W$, which are in
  particular elements of $V$, so they are inherited from $V$; likewise
  associativity and commutativity of the restricted addition;
- $0_V$ lies in $W$ by (W1) and is a two-sided identity for the restricted
  addition, since it is one in $V$;
- for $v \in W$ the vector $(-1_F)v$ lies in $W$ by (W3), and
  $(-1_F)v = -v$ ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), so $-v \in W$
  and $v + (-v) = 0_V$ holds in $W$.

So $(W,+,0_V)$ is an abelian group, which is axiom (V1), and $W$ is a vector
space over $F$ **whose zero vector and whose additive inverses are those of
$V$**. In the language of [[def-subgroup]], the three displayed conditions
(S1) $0_V \in W$, (S2) closure under addition and (S3) closure under additive
inverses all hold, so $W$ is a subgroup of the abelian group $(V,+,0_V)$
([[def-group]]); that reading, and its converse, are recorded as
[[lem-linear-subspace-is-a-subgroup]] and are cited from there rather than
re-argued below.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]). As in
[[def-linear-combination-and-span]], a **finite list** of vectors is a function
$v : n \to V$ on a von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), written
$v_i := v(i)$, and

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$$

is the finite sum of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] read additively in the abelian
group $(V,+,0_V)$, applied to the list $i \mapsto \lambda_i v_i$. No second notion
of finite sum is introduced here.

### Independence of a list

A finite list $v : n \to V$ is **linearly independent** when, for every list of
scalars $\lambda : n \to F$,

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i = 0_V \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \lambda_i = 0_F \text{ for every } i < n,$$

and **linearly dependent** otherwise, that is, when some $\lambda : n \to F$ has
$\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i = 0_V$ while $\lambda_j \ne 0_F$ for at least one
$j < n$. Such a $\lambda$ is called a **witness** to the dependence of $v$.

### Independence of a subset

A subset $S \subseteq V$ is **linearly independent** when **every injective**
finite list $v : n \to S$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]) is linearly
independent, and **linearly dependent** otherwise, that is, when some injective
finite list into $S$ is linearly dependent.

**The injectivity clause is not decoration.** A linear combination in
[[def-linear-combination-and-span]] is indexed by an arbitrary list $v : n \to S$,
which is **not** required to be injective. If the definition above quantified
over all such lists, then for any $w \in S$ the list $v : 2 \to S$ with
$v_0 = v_1 = w$ and the scalars $\lambda_0 = 1_F$, $\lambda_1 = -1_F$ would give

$$\sum_{i<2}\lambda_i v_i = (0_V + 1_F w) + (-1_F)w = w + (-w) = 0_V$$

with $\lambda_0 = 1_F \ne 0_F$ ([[def-field]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), so **every** nonempty subset of
$V$ would be dependent and the notion would be empty. Quantifying over injective
lists is what makes the subset notion the intended one. It costs nothing for
lists: [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]] shows that the vanishing condition
above already forces a list to be injective, so no injectivity hypothesis has to
be carried alongside independence of a list.

### The boundary cases are genuine cases

$\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so both of the following are
instances of the definitions and neither is a convention.

- **The empty list is independent.** For $n = 0$ the only list of scalars is the
  empty one, and the condition "$\lambda_i = 0_F$ for every $i < 0$" holds
  vacuously.
- **$\varnothing \subseteq V$ is independent.** The only function $v : n \to
  \varnothing$ is the empty one, with $n = 0$, and it is independent by the
  previous point.
- **$\{0_V\}$ is dependent.** The list $v : 1 \to \{0_V\}$ with $v_0 = 0_V$ is
  injective, and taking $\lambda_0 = 1_F$ gives
  $\sum_{i<1}\lambda_i v_i = 0_V + 1_F 0_V = 0_V$ by the recursion of
  [[def-monoid-finite-product]] and $\lambda 0_V = 0_V$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), while $1_F \ne 0_F$ in a field
  ([[def-field]]). So $\{0_V\}$, and hence every subset of $V$ containing $0_V$,
  is linearly dependent.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) and let
$S \subseteq V$. Write

$$L(S) \;:=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i \;:\; n \in \mathbb{N},\ \lambda : n \to F,\ v : n \to S \,\Bigr\}$$

for the set of linear combinations of elements of $S$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]). Then

$$\operatorname{span}(S) \;=\; L(S).$$

In particular $\operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$, and for every
$S \subseteq V$ the span of $S$ contains $0_V$ as the empty linear combination.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

A subset $B \subseteq V$ is a **basis of $V$** when

- **(B1)** $B$ is linearly independent ([[def-linear-independence]]), and
- **(B2)** $B$ spans $V$, that is $\operatorname{span}(B) = V$
  ([[def-linear-combination-and-span]], which is where the words *spans* and
  *spanning set* are fixed; they are not redefined here).

**The empty set is a basis of the zero space, and of nothing else.**
$\varnothing$ is linearly independent ([[def-linear-independence]]) and
$\operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]]), so $\varnothing$ is a basis of
$V$ exactly when $V = \{0_V\}$. This is the case $n = 0$ from which every
induction on this page starts, and it is a genuine case rather than a convention.

### Ordered bases

An **ordered basis of $V$** is a finite list $v : n \to V$, with $n \in
\mathbb{N}$ and $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ the von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), such that $v$ is
injective ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]) and its image $v[n]$ is a
basis of $V$.

By claim 6 of [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]], a list is linearly
independent exactly when it is injective with linearly independent image, so an
ordered basis is equally described as a **linearly independent list $v : n \to V$
with $\operatorname{span}(v[n]) = V$**: the injectivity does not have to be
imposed separately. The empty list is the ordered basis of the zero space.

An ordered basis is a list, so it carries an order; a basis is a set, so it does
not. Reordering an ordered basis gives a different ordered basis with the same
image, and the coordinates of
[[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] are attached to the
list, not to the set.

### Bases of a linear subspace

Let $U$ be a linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]), which is itself a
vector space over $F$, with the addition, the zero vector and the scalar
multiplication of $V$ restricted to $U$. For $A \subseteq U$ the two readings of
"$A$ is a basis" — computed inside $U$, or computed inside $V$ — agree, so the
phrase needs no disambiguation below.

- **Independence agrees.** The finite sums $\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i a_i$ of a list
  $a : n \to U$ are given by the same recursion in $U$ as in $V$
  ([[def-monoid-finite-product]]), the base value $0_V$ and the operation $+$
  being literally those of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). So a list into $U$ has
  the same sums whichever space it is read in, and the vanishing condition of
  [[def-linear-independence]] is the same condition in both.
- **The span agrees.** A subset of $U$ is a linear subspace of $U$ exactly when it
  is a linear subspace of $V$, conditions (W1), (W2), (W3) being the same
  conditions in either reading. Now $\operatorname{span}_V(A) \subseteq U$, since
  $U$ is a linear subspace of $V$ containing $A$ and the span is contained in
  every such subspace; so $\operatorname{span}_V(A)$ is a linear subspace of $U$
  containing $A$, whence $\operatorname{span}_U(A) \subseteq \operatorname{span}_V(A)$.
  Conversely $\operatorname{span}_U(A)$ is a linear subspace of $V$ containing
  $A$, whence $\operatorname{span}_V(A) \subseteq \operatorname{span}_U(A)$. The
  two are therefore equal, and we write $\operatorname{span}(A)$ for both.

Consequently $A \subseteq U$ is a basis of the vector space $U$ if and only if
$A$ is linearly independent as a subset of $V$ and $\operatorname{span}(A) = U$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

$V$ is **finite-dimensional over $F$** when it has a **finite** basis
([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-countable]]): some basis $B$ of $V$ satisfies
$B \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]).

For such a $V$, the **dimension of $V$ over $F$**, written $\dim_F V$, is that
$n$:

$$\dim_F V \;:=\; \text{the unique } n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } V \text{ has a basis } B \text{ with } B \approx n .$$

**This is well defined.** Existence of such an $n$ is the hypothesis, together
with the fact that a finite set is equinumerous with exactly one natural number
([[lem-pigeonhole]], claim 3). Uniqueness is
[[thm-any-two-finite-bases-have-the-same-size]]: two bases of $V$ with $n$ and
with $m$ elements force $n = m$. That theorem is therefore a **prerequisite** of
this definition, not a later justification of it, and it is listed in `deps`.

$V$ is **infinite-dimensional over $F$** when it is not finite-dimensional over
$F$, that is, when $V$ has **no** finite basis. No number is attached to such a
space here: the symbol $\dim_F V$ is defined only in the finite-dimensional case,
and the expression $\dim_F V = \infty$ is not used.

**The zero space.** $\varnothing$ is a basis of $\{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-basis]]) and $\varnothing \approx 0$, so $\{0_V\}$ is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F \{0_V\} = 0$. Conversely a space of dimension $0$
has a basis $B \approx 0$, that is $B = \varnothing$, and then
$V = \operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

Then $s\cdot u^{(i)}=s_i\oplus(s_j\land s_i)=s_i\oplus s_i=0$, so every $u^{(i)}$ belongs to $s^\perp$. When $n=1$, the index set $i\ne j$ is empty.

For any $y\in s^\perp$, the equation $s\cdot y=0$ and $s_j=1$ give $y_j= igoplus_{i
e j}(s_i\land y_i)$; hence $y=\sum_{i

$$f(x)=f(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (y=x\text{ or }y=x\oplus s).$$

For the query algorithms using this promise, the instance is $n,m$ together with black-box access to $f$: the solver receives no function table or other information depending on $f$. Each oracle call uses the standard bit-query interface [[def-qa-standard-bit-query]]. A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

Since $m\ge n-1$, $L=2^m\ge C$, and the number of injections from a $C$-element set into an $L$-element set is $L(L-1)\cdots(L-C+1)>0$, the sample space is finite and nonempty.

Give every pair $(s,\lambda)$ weight $1/((2^n-1)L(L-1)\cdots(L-C+1))$. There are exactly the denominator's many pairs, so the weights are nonnegative and sum to one by [F2]. Because the number of injections is constant for each $s$, the induced hidden mask is uniform and, conditional on it, every injection is equally likely.

If $x\oplus s=y$, the two addresses lie in the same coset and receive the same label. Conversely, if $f_{s,\lambda}(x)=f_{s,\lambda}(y)$, injectivity of $\lambda$ gives equal cosets, hence $y=x$ or $y=x\oplus s$. Since $s\ne0$, this is exactly the Simon promise with unique hidden mask $s$.

$$
U_f|x\rangle|y\rangle=|x\rangle|y\oplus f(x)\rangle
$$
on the ordered $a$-bit address register followed by the ordered $b$-bit target register. Here $\oplus$ is componentwise addition modulo two, and words label the ordered computational basis as in [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] and [[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]]. 2. Apply the standard bit-flip oracle $U_f|x\rangle|z\rangle=|x\rangle|z\oplus f(x)\rangle$ once. Measure the target with the computational-basis projective measurement [[def-qc-projective-measurement]], viewed as the finite POVM [[def-qc-povm-and-outcome-law]]. Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Its **endomorphisms** are its complex-linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]); for an endomorphism $P$, $P^*$ denotes its adjoint, which exists uniquely in finite dimension ([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]], [[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]]). A **finite projective measurement** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $(P_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ of endomorphisms such that

$$P_a^*=P_a,\qquad P_a^2=P_a,\qquad P_aP_b=0\ (a\ne b),\qquad \sum_{a\in\Omega}P_a=I_H.$$

The products above are compositions, the sum is pointwise addition of endomorphisms, and $I_H$ is the identity map; these operations preserve linear maps ([[prop-linear-maps-form-a-vector-space]], [[lem-composition-and-identity-linear-maps]]). The projections $P_a=0$ are permitted. For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (nonnegative and trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), the associated outcome weights are $p_\rho(a)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_a)$; their nonnegativity and normalization are proved in [[thm-qc-projective-measurement-outcome-law]].

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space; the pairing is linear in its first argument ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for its complex-linear endomorphisms ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]) and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite POVM** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $E=(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ with each $E_a$ nonnegative and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}E_a=I_H$; after any enumeration of $\Omega$, these operators form the finite complete positive family of [[def-qc-finite-positive-effect-family]]. Reordering does not alter the finite sum. The complete-family lemma [[lem-qc-complete-effect-family-members-are-effects]] shows that every $E_a$ also has nonnegative complement $I_H-E_a$, so each is an effect.

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (a nonnegative operator of trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), its **POVM outcome weights** are

$$p_\rho(a):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a),\qquad a\in\Omega.$$

Here $\operatorname{tr}$ is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

The positivity and normalization of these weights are proved in [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]]. A POVM specifies this outcome law; it does not by itself prescribe a conditional output state.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Let $(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ be a finite POVM on $H$, and let $M_a=E_a^{1/2}$ be the nonnegative square root of each effect. The maps

$$\mathcal I_a(X):=M_aXM_a,\qquad X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

form an instrument from $H$ to itself.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space, let $K$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space, and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite instrument** from $H$ to $K$ is a family of complex-linear maps $\mathcal I_a:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$, one for each $a\in\Omega$, such that each $\mathcal I_a$ is completely positive ([[def-qc-completely-positive-map]]) and

$$\sum_{a\in\Omega}\operatorname{tr}_K(\mathcal I_a(X))=\operatorname{tr}_H(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H).$$

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (nonnegative with trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), define the outcome weight $p_a(\rho):=\operatorname{tr}_K(\mathcal I_a(\rho))$. The **conditional state** for outcome $a$ is

$$\rho_a:=\begin{cases}\mathcal I_a(\rho)/p_a(\rho),&p_a(\rho)>0,\\[2pt]\bot,&p_a(\rho)=0.\end{cases}$$

Here $\bot$ is a symbol meaning that no conditional density operator is assigned; it is not a state. Positivity and normalization of the outcome weights, and density of every positive-probability conditional state, are proved in [[thm-qc-instrument-outcome-law-normalizes]] and [[thm-qc-instrument-conditional-state-is-density]].

For a finite instrument $(\mathcal I_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ and a density operator $\rho$ on its input space, the branch weights $p_a=\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal I_a(\rho))$ form a probability distribution on $\Omega$.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

$$

where $H$ is the exact one-qubit gate of [[def-qc-one-qubit-gate-alphabet-and-rotations]] and tensor factors follow the ordered register convention of [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]].

Define $P_u:=|u\rangle\langle u|$ by the root-linear-first Dirac convention. Then $P_u$ is self-adjoint and idempotent, has one-dimensional range, is non-negative, and has trace one. 2. If such $i$ exists, swap rows $i$ and $k$. For every other row $r\ne k$ with entry $1$ in column $j$, replace row $r$ by its bitwise XOR with row $k$. Record $j$ as a pivot column and increase $k$ by one.

The quotient operations on $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ make the carrier $\mathbb F_2$ of [[def-qa-binary-field-f2]] a field. This is only the modulus-$2$ specialization of the published prime-modulus theorem; it does not assert a classification of finite fields.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

Fix integers $n\ge1$ and $m\ge n-1$. A total function $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^m$ satisfies the **Simon hidden-XOR-period promise** if there is a unique nonzero string $s\in\{0,1\}^n$ such that for all $x,y\in\{0,1\}^n$,

$$f(x)=f(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (y=x\text{ or }y=x\oplus s).$$

For the query algorithms using this promise, the instance is $n,m$ together with black-box access to $f$: the solver receives no function table or other information depending on $f$. Each oracle call uses the standard bit-query interface [[def-qa-standard-bit-query]]. Its witness relation $R(f,s)$ holds exactly when $s$ is the nonzero mask in the displayed iff condition, so the required output is the unique hidden mask. The address operation $\oplus$ is the coordinatewise addition of [[def-qa-binary-field-f2]]. The output width condition lets the $2^{n-1}$ fibers receive distinct labels; it does not promise that the image uses every $m$-bit label. Each fiber is exactly $\{x,x\oplus s\}$.

For $n\ge0$ and $a,x\in\{0,1\}^{n}$, define the one-bit **binary dot product**
$$
a\cdot x:=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{n-1}(a_i\land x_i),
$$
where $\land$ is Boolean conjunction and $\bigoplus$ is the left-to-right fold of XOR, with empty fold $0$. It is the parity of the number of coordinates where both bits are $1$. Under the quotient operations of [[def-qa-binary-field-f2]], this bit represents the sum $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}[a_i]_2[x_i]_2$ in $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$; the equality uses only the operation definitions, not the field axioms.
Every finite matrix over a field is row equivalent to a matrix in row echelon form. The reduction can be obtained by the Gaussian elimination algorithm.

For a classical query algorithm [[def-qa-classical-query-algorithm]], bit-operation cost is the number of transitions of a declared multitape Turing machine over a fixed finite alphabet; the $k$-tape transition reads and writes one symbol on each of its $k\ge1$ tapes and moves each head once per transition ([[def-multitape-and-nondeterministic-machines]]). It includes random-bit generation, any encoding work actually performed by that machine on declared public data or received replies, address formation, reading and writing every bit of an oracle reply, comparison/postprocessing, and writing the classical output. The abstract instance encoding in [[def-qa-input-encoding-and-size]] fixes the size parameter; it supplies neither a readable hidden input nor an encoding procedure to execute. The fair-bit machine convention is supplied by [[def-probabilistic-polynomial-time-machine-interface]]. The oracle invocation itself is one separately counted query action; its returned bits are not free to process.

For a query with an $a(n)$-bit address and a $b(n)$-bit reply, the machine's charged work includes forming the address and processing the $b(n)$ reply symbols. A claimed time bound also specifies whether it is worst-case over promised inputs and random tapes, as in [[def-probabilistic-polynomial-time-machine-interface]]. Query, nonoracle quantum gate, measurement, and classical bit costs remain distinct.

For $n\ge0$, let $\mathbb F_2^n=\{0,1\}^n$. Give it coordinatewise addition $(x+y)_i=x_i+y_i$ and scalar multiplication $(c x)_i=cx_i$ using the operations of [[def-qa-binary-field-f2]]. Its zero vector is $0^n$. Then $\mathbb F_2^n$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F_2$, with standard basis $e_0,\ldots,e_{n-1}$ and dimension $n$. For $n=0$, the carrier consists of the empty tuple, and the basis is empty.

Let $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and let $b\in F^m$, viewed as an $m\times1$ column. The **matrix equation** $Ax=b$ asks for columns $x\in F^n$ satisfying the displayed equality. Equivalently it is the linear system
$$\sum_{j<n}a_{ij}x_j=b_i\qquad(i<m).$$

Its **solution set** is $S(A,b):=\{x\in F^n:Ax=b\}$. The system is **consistent** when $S(A,b)\ne\varnothing$ and **inconsistent** otherwise. It is **homogeneous** when $b=0$.

The **augmented matrix** is $[A\mid b]\in M_{m\times(n+1)}(F)$, obtained by adjoining $b$ as the last column. Elementary row operations act on every entry of a row, including its augmented entry.
For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, the matrix rank of $A$ equals the rank of the linear map $L_A:F^n\to F^m$ defined by $L_A(x)=Ax$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

A subset $B \subseteq V$ is a **basis of $V$** when

- **(B1)** $B$ is linearly independent ([[def-linear-independence]]), and
- **(B2)** $B$ spans $V$, that is $\operatorname{span}(B) = V$
  ([[def-linear-combination-and-span]], which is where the words *spans* and
  *spanning set* are fixed; they are not redefined here).

**The empty set is a basis of the zero space, and of nothing else.**
$\varnothing$ is linearly independent ([[def-linear-independence]]) and
$\operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]]), so $\varnothing$ is a basis of
$V$ exactly when $V = \{0_V\}$. This is the case $n = 0$ from which every
induction on this page starts, and it is a genuine case rather than a convention.

### Ordered bases

An **ordered basis of $V$** is a finite list $v : n \to V$, with $n \in
\mathbb{N}$ and $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ the von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), such that $v$ is
injective ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]) and its image $v[n]$ is a
basis of $V$.

By claim 6 of [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]], a list is linearly
independent exactly when it is injective with linearly independent image, so an
ordered basis is equally described as a **linearly independent list $v : n \to V$
with $\operatorname{span}(v[n]) = V$**: the injectivity does not have to be
imposed separately. The empty list is the ordered basis of the zero space.

An ordered basis is a list, so it carries an order; a basis is a set, so it does
not. Reordering an ordered basis gives a different ordered basis with the same
image, and the coordinates of
[[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] are attached to the
list, not to the set.

### Bases of a linear subspace

Let $U$ be a linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]), which is itself a
vector space over $F$, with the addition, the zero vector and the scalar
multiplication of $V$ restricted to $U$. For $A \subseteq U$ the two readings of
"$A$ is a basis" — computed inside $U$, or computed inside $V$ — agree, so the
phrase needs no disambiguation below.

- **Independence agrees.** The finite sums $\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i a_i$ of a list
  $a : n \to U$ are given by the same recursion in $U$ as in $V$
  ([[def-monoid-finite-product]]), the base value $0_V$ and the operation $+$
  being literally those of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). So a list into $U$ has
  the same sums whichever space it is read in, and the vanishing condition of
  [[def-linear-independence]] is the same condition in both.
- **The span agrees.** A subset of $U$ is a linear subspace of $U$ exactly when it
  is a linear subspace of $V$, conditions (W1), (W2), (W3) being the same
  conditions in either reading. Now $\operatorname{span}_V(A) \subseteq U$, since
  $U$ is a linear subspace of $V$ containing $A$ and the span is contained in
  every such subspace; so $\operatorname{span}_V(A)$ is a linear subspace of $U$
  containing $A$, whence $\operatorname{span}_U(A) \subseteq \operatorname{span}_V(A)$.
  Conversely $\operatorname{span}_U(A)$ is a linear subspace of $V$ containing
  $A$, whence $\operatorname{span}_V(A) \subseteq \operatorname{span}_U(A)$. The
  two are therefore equal, and we write $\operatorname{span}(A)$ for both.

Consequently $A \subseteq U$ is a basis of the vector space $U$ if and only if
$A$ is linearly independent as a subset of $V$ and $\operatorname{span}(A) = U$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) and let
$S \subseteq V$. Write

$$L(S) \;:=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i \;:\; n \in \mathbb{N},\ \lambda : n \to F,\ v : n \to S \,\Bigr\}$$

for the set of linear combinations of elements of $S$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]). Then

$$\operatorname{span}(S) \;=\; L(S).$$

In particular $\operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$, and for every
$S \subseteq V$ the span of $S$ contains $0_V$ as the empty linear combination.

Set
$$
\mathbb F_2:=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z=\{[0]_2,[1]_2\},
$$
with addition and multiplication induced by the quotient operations
$$
[r]_2+[s]_2=[r+s]_2,\qquad [r]_2[s]_2=[rs]_2
$$
from [[def-addition-and-multiplication-modulo-n]]. This item fixes the two residue classes and their operations. It does not assert the field axioms; those must be established separately before an argument uses field properties.

Let $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$. Its **row space** $\operatorname{Row}(A)\subseteq F^n$ is the span of its rows, its **column space** $\operatorname{Col}(A)\subseteq F^m$ is the span of its columns, and its **nullspace** is
$$N(A):=\{x\in F^n:Ax=0\}.$$

The **row rank** and **column rank** are
$$\operatorname{rrank}(A):=\dim_F\operatorname{Row}(A),\qquad \operatorname{crank}(A):=\dim_F\operatorname{Col}(A).$$
These dimensions are defined because each space is spanned by a finite list.
Starting with the empty list, inspect the spanning vectors in order and retain a
vector exactly when it is not in the span of those already retained. Induction
shows that the retained list is independent and has the same span as the
original finite list, so it is a finite basis. The **rank** of $A$ is its row
rank; [[thm-row-rank-equals-column-rank]] proves that it also equals the column
rank.

derivations.claim: Swapping two rows or replacing a row by its XOR with another preserves both the homogeneous solution set and row space: each operation has an inverse of the same form, and the new row is a combination of old rows. Thus the rank and kernel of $Y$ are preserved by [F13] and [F9]. The loops visit $n$ columns and at most $n-1$ pivot rows, with finite row scans, so they terminate.

At each pivot the selected entry is $1$, earlier pivot columns are zero below it, and XORing the pivot row clears its column in every other row. At termination the pivot columns form an identity block and all remaining rows are zero. The nonzero rows are independent because their pivot columns form an identity matrix, and they span the row space because every other row is zero. By [F13], the pivot count equals $\operatorname{rank}(Y)$; step 1.1 preserves this rank from the input. The procedure returns FAIL precisely when this rank is below $n-1$.

If the pivot count is $n-1$, there is exactly one nonpivot column. Setting its coordinate to $1$ and solving each pivot equation gives a vector in the reduced system with that coordinate nonzero. By step 1.1, it lies in the kernel of the original $Y$ and is nonzero.

Whenever $\operatorname{rank}(Y)=n-1$, the associated map has rank $n-1$ by [F10] and domain dimension $n$ by [F8]; rank-nullity [F3] gives a one-dimensional kernel. A basis of that kernel has one vector $u$, so every vector is $c u$ by [F11]; [F12] gives $c\in\{0,1\}$, hence $u$ is its unique nonzero vector. The algorithm's output from step 3.1 is therefore the unique nonzero kernel vector. In the Simon case, every row has dot product zero with $s$, so [F5] and [F9] give $s\in\ker Y$, and [F4] gives $s\ne0$; thus the output is $s$.

Store the $n-1$ rows consecutively on an input work tape. To find pivots, a multitape machine may scan the whole $O(n^2)$-bit matrix once for each of at most $n$ columns; this costs $O(n^3)$ transitions including head movement. For each of at most $n-1$ pivots, copy its $n$ bits to a work tape, then scan each of at most $n-2$ other rows and XOR the copied pivot row into it when required; each scan and row update costs $O(n)$ transitions, so all row operations cost $O(n^3)$. Swaps, pivot bookkeeping, and back-substitution require at most $O(n^3)$ further transitions under the same scan representation. The finite-alphabet multitape convention [F7] therefore gives the stated $O(n^3)$ classical bit cost.

Fix $n\ge1$ and $m\ge n-1$, and put $L=2^m$ and $C=2^{n-1}$. Choose $s$ uniformly from the $2^n-1$ nonzero binary masks. Let $\mathcal C_s$ be the set of address pairs $\{x,x\oplus s\}$. Conditional on $s$, choose uniformly an injection $\lambda:\mathcal C_s\to\{0,1\}^m$ and define the total oracle $f_{s,\lambda}(x)=\lambda(\{x,x\oplus s\})$.

The sample space consists of all pairs $(s,\lambda)$ with equal weight. There are $C$ cosets and $L\ge C$ labels, so each $s$ admits exactly $L(L-1)\cdots(L-C+1)$ injections; this number does not depend on $s$. Thus the marginal on $s$ is uniform and the conditional label assignment is uniform without replacement.

A **classical query algorithm** is a finite decision procedure for a fixed encoded instance length $n$ and explicitly declared public data $p$, whose query actions are to the total function $f_z$ of [[def-qa-promise-query-instance]]. The procedure is fixed independently of the hidden instance $z$ at fixed $(n,p)$. Its encoding in [[def-qa-input-encoding-and-size]] labels the instance and determines its size; it does not provide a readable copy of the hidden encoding. Each query chooses an address from $n,p$, earlier replies, and any random bits used so far; it receives the entire $b(n)$-bit reply $f_z(x)$ as one query answer. The address choices may be adaptive. Its terminal output is determined by the same public data, replies, and random tape.

In the ordinary oracle-only model, all dependence on the hidden instance is through these replies. Public parameters such as register widths, a supplied marked count, or an explicit arithmetic input may be used only when the task declares them. A lower bound in the oracle-only model fixes the declared public data across the hidden instances it compares. Additional input-access or preparation capabilities must be explicitly declared with their charges; they are extra resources, not supplied by the hidden instance encoding.

For a randomized algorithm, each branch is determined by the public data, oracle replies, and its finite random tape; the fair-bit tape convention for a bounded-time probabilistic machine is supplied by [[def-probabilistic-polynomial-time-machine-interface]]. The query model itself imposes no polynomial bit-time bound. A query bound is a worst-case bound over promised inputs and every random branch; classical computation between queries is charged separately only when a bit-cost model is specified.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

derivations.claim: Assume, for contradiction, that $q\le\lfloor\sqrt N/4\rfloor$. Put $S=N-1$ and $B=\binom q2$.

Fix one finite random tape, making the algorithm deterministic. Repeated addresses can be answered from the earlier reply and removed without changing the output, so the resulting at most $q$ queries are distinct.
The assumption in step 1.1 gives $B\le q^2/2\le N/32$. Hence $S-B\ge31N/32-1>0$, since $N=2^n\ge256$.

Consider a collision-free transcript of $t\le q$ queries. A mask is inconsistent with it only if it is the XOR difference of a pair of queried addresses, so at most $\binom t2\le B$ masks are excluded and at least $S-B$ remain. For each remaining $s$, the queried addresses lie in distinct $s$-cosets. Write $(L)_t=L(L-1)\cdots(L-t+1)$, where $L=2^m$ and $C=2^{n-1}$. For a specified ordered list of $t$ distinct replies, the number of injections extending those assignments is $(L-t)_{C-t}$ out of $(L)_C$ total injections, giving likelihood $1/(L)_t$, independent of $s$. Because the deterministic query addresses are functions of earlier replies, the transcript has the same likelihood for every consistent mask. The posterior on those masks is therefore uniform.

At the $j$th fresh query, a collision with a previous address $x_i$ requires $s=x_j\oplus x_i$. There are at most $j-1$ candidate masks, and after any collision-free transcript at least $S-B$ masks remain equally likely by step 3.1. Thus the probability that the first collision occurs at query $j$ is at most $(j-1)/(S-B)$. Summing over $j=2,\ldots,q$ bounds the total collision probability by $\sum_{j=2}^q(j-1)/(S-B)=B/(S-B)$.

On a collision-free transcript, the deterministic final guess is correct with probability at most $1/(S-B)$, since at least that many masks remain equally likely. On transcripts with a collision, success is at most one. Therefore average success under [F1] is at most $B/(S-B)+1/(S-B)=(B+1)/(S-B)$.

By steps 1.1 and 2.2, with $S-B>0$, $(B+1)/(S-B)\le(N/32+1)/(31N/32-1)<2/3$. The strict inequality is equivalent to $5<59N/32$, which holds because $N\ge256$. Thus every fixed random tape has average success strictly below $2/3$ under the finite oracle distribution.

Averaging over the algorithm's finite random tapes keeps its average success below $2/3$. But success at least $2/3$ on every promised function implies average success at least $2/3$ under [F1], since every function in that distribution is promised. This contradiction proves $q>\lfloor\sqrt N/4\rfloor$ and hence the stated $\Omega(2^{n/2})$ lower bound.

For a Simon oracle with hidden nonzero string $s$, immediately after its one standard query the joint state is

$$2^{-n/2}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}|x\rangle|f(x)\rangle.$$

For each output value $v$ in the image of $f$, the target Lüders instrument has probability $2^{1-n}$ and its conditional joint state factors as

$$\frac{|x_0\rangle+|x_0\oplus s\rangle}{\sqrt2}\otimes|v\rangle,$$

where $x_0$ is either preimage of $v$. Outcomes outside the image have probability zero. Hence the address register conditional state is the normalized coset-pair vector shown above.

For $n\ge1$ and $z\in\{0,1\}^n$, with the binary dot product of [[def-qa-binary-dot-product]],
$$
\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}(-1)^{x\cdot z}=\begin{cases}2^n,&z=0^n,\\0,&z\ne0^n.\end{cases}
$$
Consequently, for every $x\in\{0,1\}^n$,
$$
H^{\otimes n}|x\rangle=2^{-n/2}\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^n}(-1)^{x\cdot y}|y\rangle,
$$
where $H$ is the exact one-qubit gate of [[def-qc-one-qubit-gate-alphabet-and-rotations]] and tensor factors follow the ordered register convention of [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]].

For $n\ge0$ and $a,x\in\{0,1\}^{n}$, define the one-bit **binary dot product**
$$
a\cdot x:=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{n-1}(a_i\land x_i),
$$
where $\land$ is Boolean conjunction and $\bigoplus$ is the left-to-right fold of XOR, with empty fold $0$. It is the parity of the number of coordinates where both bits are $1$. Under the quotient operations of [[def-qa-binary-field-f2]], this bit represents the sum $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}[a_i]_2[x_i]_2$ in $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$; the equality uses only the operation definitions, not the field axioms.

**Input:** Integers $n\ge1$, $m\ge n-1$, and ordinary access through the [[def-qa-standard-bit-query]] to a total function satisfying [[def-qa-simon-promise]]. Prepare an ordered $n$-qubit address register and $m$-qubit target register, both in their zero computational-basis states.

**Instructions:**

1. Apply the exact one-qubit Hadamard gate to every address wire, producing $H^{\otimes n}|0^n\rangle$, and leave the target at $|0^m\rangle$.
2. Apply the standard bit-flip oracle $U_f|x\rangle|z\rangle=|x\rangle|z\oplus f(x)\rangle$ once. Measure the target with the computational-basis projective measurement [[def-qc-projective-measurement]], viewed as the finite POVM [[def-qc-povm-and-outcome-law]]. Use the Lüders branch maps $\mathcal I_v(X)=P_vXP_v$, where $P_v=I_{\rm address}\otimes|v\rangle\langle v|$, under the instrument and conditional-state interface [[def-qc-instrument-and-conditional-state]]. Theorem [[thm-qc-luders-instrument-of-a-povm-is-valid]] supplies a valid instrument; its outcome weights and positive-branch states are covered by [[thm-qc-instrument-outcome-law-normalizes]] and [[thm-qc-instrument-conditional-state-is-density]]. Discard the reported value and target register. The POVM effects are these same $P_v$.
3. Apply $H^{\otimes n}$ to the address register and measure it in the computational basis. Return the observed $n$-bit string $y$ as one sample row.

Every branch uses exactly one oracle query and $2n$ Hadamard gates. It makes one finite instrument measurement on the target and one terminal projective measurement on the address. The intermediate target outcome is not used by classical postprocessing. There is no failure branch, controlled-oracle call, or inverse-oracle call. This procedure's sample law is proved separately in [[thm-qa-simon-hadamard-sampling-law]].

Let $(|y\rangle)_{y\in\mathcal Y}$ be a finite ordered orthonormal computational basis, let $\psi=\sum_{y\in\mathcal Y}a_y|y\rangle$ be a unit vector, and put $\rho=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$. For the computational-basis projective measurement with $P_y=|y\rangle\langle y|$, the associated POVM weight is
$$
p(y)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_y)=|a_y|^2.
$$
In particular these weights are nonnegative and sum to one.
